source: OECD (2025), Health at a Glance 2025: OECD Indicators, OECD Publishing, Paris
framing: Gap framing: every figure is what is NOT covered, NOT satisfied or unmet. Gap figures are 100 minus the published figure.
rule: HAL may phrase these facts freely but must not state any figure, ranking or claim that is not in this list. Verbatim report sentences may name other countries; only what they say about this country may be used.

facts.text: 38% of people in Estonia were NOT satisfied with the availability of quality healthcare where they live in 2024, versus an OECD average of 36%.
24.2% of health spending in Estonia was NOT covered by government or compulsory insurance schemes in 2023, versus an OECD average of 24.9%.
8.5% of people in Estonia reported unmet medical care needs due to cost, distance or waiting times in 2024 (average of 28 OECD countries: 3.4%).
1% of hospital care costs in Estonia were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 11% on average in the OECD.
16% of outpatient medical care costs in Estonia were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 22% on average in the OECD.
72% of dental care costs in Estonia were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 68% on average in the OECD.
43% of pharmaceutical costs in Estonia were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 42% on average in the OECD.

While satisfaction levels have decreased on average across OECD countries over the past decade, this masks wide cross-country variation: Türkiye experienced the largest decline in satisfaction of 30 percentage points (percentage points), while Canada, France and New Zealand also had declines of over 20 percentage points Conversely, in Chile and Estonia satisfaction levels increased by 10 percentage points or more.

However, over 8% of the population reported unmet care needs in Latvia (8.4%), Estonia (8.5%), Finland (8.6%), Canada (9.1%) and Greece (12.1%), while in Germany, the Netherlands and Czechia, fewer than 1% of the population reported unmet needs for medical care.
In Latvia, Estonia and Finland, more than 5% of the population cited waiting times as a barrier.

In Greece, more than one in six people in the lowest income quintile reported unmet medical care needs, and in Estonia, Finland and Latvia this proportion reaches more than one in ten people in the lowest income quintile.

In many countries, patients have access to free acute inpatient care or only need to make a small copayment; as a result, coverage rates were near 100% in Sweden, Norway, Iceland and Estonia, as well as accession country Romania.

Teleconsultations comprised over 25% of all doctor consultations in Denmark, Estonia, Israel, Portugal and Sweden, but remained very low in Chile, Germany, Greece and Korea (see the section on “Data and digital” in Chapter 9 for trends in teleconsultations).
Taken together, in 2023, spending on outpatient care services accounted for around 45% of all health spending in Israel, Portugal and Estonia compared to an OECD average of 33%.

In 2023, PHC represented 14% of all health spending on average across OECD countries, ranging from 10% or less in Switzerland, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and the Slovak Republic to around 20% in Lithuania, Estonia and Finland (Figure 7.16).
In Lithuania and Estonia, the large share of PHC in overall health spending can be explained by spending on dental care.
